Question: My boss offered me a role with more responsibility with no increase in pay, implying it's "good for your career" and that my chances of a raise are higher, what would you think/do?
Old_Answer: Take it. Make sure it comes with a better title. If you don't eventually get more pay commensurate with your new position, your boss has at least given you the ticket to getting more pay at your next employer. More responsibility is generally very good for your career regardless of pay. There is a question if you want to do that job that you will have to answer for yourself, but this is a good career move on all other accounts. Few companies will ever hire you into a higher position then the one you are leaving unless they are a startup and desperate. Other companies will almost certainly pay you more though if they want you. What you have been given is priceless in terms of career development. Worry about the money after you have delivered on your new title and find yourself undervalued and with new opportunity to get more pay elsewhere.
Answer_with_writing_sample: That's a tricky situation, and it’s important to weigh the pros and cons carefully. On one hand, taking on more responsibility can indeed be a valuable experience that enhances your skills and makes you more marketable in the long run. It could open doors for future opportunities, especially if you can demonstrate your capability in a more challenging role. However, the lack of immediate financial compensation raises a red flag. It’s essential to consider whether this new role aligns with your career goals and if the promised raise is a realistic expectation or just a vague hope. You might want to have a candid conversation with your boss about your concerns. Ask for clarity on what "good for your career" means in tangible terms and how they plan to support you in this transition. It’s also reasonable to discuss the possibility of a salary review after a certain period in the new role, especially if you’re taking on significantly more work. Ultimately, you need to feel valued and fairly compensated for your contributions. If the role seems like a stepping stone that aligns with your aspirations and you can negotiate some form of assurance regarding future pay, it might be worth considering. If not, it could be a sign to explore other opportunities where your skills and efforts will be recognized and rewarded appropriately.

Question: What do liberal progressives think about the living conditions in San Francisco?
Old_Answer: Ugh. It turns out the romanticized moral of the story of David vs Goliath is, in general, profoundly bad. San Francisco is your evidence. It turns out, big slow moving entities that sometimes harm the little guy often do so for the greater good. The proverbial David may have been smaller and protecting a minority, but he crushed Goliath then used his righteous indignation as justification to force his Christian identity on the Pagan majority. A similar thing happens in San Francisco. I was driving through the city this weekend, coming from the south bay. I didn’t want to do anything in the city, just get through it as quickly as possible. That’s just not possible. San Francisco hates cars. I do too, but that doesn’t change the reality we currently live in. California has been seeing massive growth for the better part of a century and seeing the problems of rapid growth during the age of the automobile is most acute here. San Francisco’s hate of cars is a long held belief thats been in place since the 60s when highway 101 and 280 was being built and had plans to cut through the west side of San Francisco. Growth and cars bring lots of problems with it. Cars may not be the best solution particularly in urban areas, but they are a net benefit over nothing. Of course more cars means lots of changes, that will have some very adverse effects on individuals. Houses would be lost, public places would be disturbed. It sucks, especially so for the handful of individuals who live in the path of that highway. I am a vocal advocate for building more public transportation and prioritizing walkability and bike lanes over highways and street parking, but I also have the common sense to realize thats a slow change that requires massive agreement on zoning and infrastructure to happen over time. Not building a single section of highway is simply not a viable option when the rest of the state has already made it the defacto transportation mechanism. The entire Bay Area is built for cars and the highways are how everyone gets around as there really are no other good options for a majority of uses case. In any case, protests in the 60s were successful. Despite the plans for the highway that were open for public comment and went through years of permitting and a drawn out planning process to find the least disruptive compromise, days before concrete was to start pouring another city council vote triggered by massive protests passed on a 6 to 5 vote cemented the lack of a highway to this day. For the perceived benefit of a handful of NIMBYs, everyone who lives in the area has to deal with significantly increased commute times. Unfortunately those protests were not “lets find a better transportation solution that works for everyone”, they simply found fault with an imperfect proposed solution and left it at that. No effort was expended to address how to better correct the worsening growth problems the solution was targeting. To this day, highway 101 ends in San Francisco, then continues after you get past it. The trouble is, even though, the highway doesn’t exist, the traffic still does. Traffic from a 12-lane highway is dumped onto city streets with lights and lots of cross traffic whether you want to end up there or not. Everyone, including the NIMBYs still lose. Ultimately the city has to deal with a massive amount of cars for longer. The noise, the pollution, the danger, the time wasted is all worse then it would of been by building a highway correctly. Cars remain in the city for more time. Public transportation also remains largely unsuccessful as the rest of the Bay Area doesn’t have the density along the transportation corridor to support it. 50 years on, demand for highways has only increased. It turns out that Goliath is big and less sympathetic to individual concerns because it has to be, not because it is inherently evil. Highways are the natural extension of how you support people who want to live in low density suburbs. That is but one anecdotal story, but it extends to the most acute problems of the Bay Area housing crisis that has become a epitome of inequality. Well intentioned individuals see a compromise and ignore the forest for a couple of trees. There is nothing wrong with caring for those individuals trees, but the government needs to care about the forest and weigh the individual losses accordingly. Individuals from every demographic can do great in the Bay Area and are protected in California, but not consistently or fairly and it comes at the expense of the vast majority who don’t have enough of an individual claim to care about. In California, political vigilantes choose a wedge issue and pursue it with blind vigor and no responsibility for the future outcome of their decisions beyond the immediate effect on their targeted special class. California has a participatory democracy that easily allows individuals to partake in legislative affairs that are normally left to city councils who have to at least have a little care about the long term repercussions of their actions on the area as a whole. This is definitely a hard sell in our current political environment, but legislation should be made by professionals who consider the long term ramifications of the issues at stake not individuals who will always be biased to what is going to effect just their own backyard. What do I think of about the living conditions in San Francisco? I think fixing the living conditions have exceedingly well-understood and viable technical solutions. However, fixing it will appear to cause a little bit of harm to a very sympathy inducing victim, long time home owners, in order to bestow a benefit to everyone including high earning new comers. David needs to lose, but no one has written a sympathetic story for that moral yet.

Question: Golang vs NodeJS vs Python? I am currently working to improve my knowledge and skill to become a back-end developer. Which should I focus more and why?
Old_Answer: All of those languages are actively used so I wouldn’t say any one was a bad choice, but there may be a better choices and better ways to make a choice. First you need to figure out what you want to do on a little more specific level then just back end developer. One way would be to look for places you want to work at with job openings. They will describe the relevant skills they are looking for as well as give you a clue as the types of projects that would be open to you. You could also pick a side project to build on your own and try it in all three languages or look for relevant examples for similar things of what you are wanting to build and pick that one that comes the easiest. In any case, pick a more tangible goal first and your choice should get much clearer.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Choosing between Golang, NodeJS, and Python for back-end development ultimately depends on your specific goals and the projects you envision working on. Golang, with its strong performance and concurrency support, is an excellent choice if you're looking to build scalable applications that can handle many simultaneous processes. Its static typing and compiled nature lead to fewer runtime errors, which can be a significant advantage in larger systems. NodeJS, on the other hand, excels in real-time applications, such as chat applications or online gaming, due to its non-blocking I/O model. If you're interested in building fast, event-driven applications, NodeJS might be the way to go. Python, with its simplicity and readability, is often recommended for beginners and is widely used in web development, data analysis, and machine learning. Its extensive libraries and frameworks, like Django and Flask, make it a versatile choice for various applications. If you’re just starting, Python might be the easiest to pick up, allowing you to quickly build projects and understand back-end concepts. However, if you're aiming for performance and scalability, Golang could be more beneficial in the long run. Ultimately, consider the type of projects you want to work on and the community support available for each language, as that can significantly impact your learning experience and career opportunities.

Old_Answer: A tax plan will almost certainly pass. We still have a year to 2018 elections and republicans will likely control all 3 branches of government after that giving them three years to make good on their promise. I expect progress this year. Question: Why don't we build park-like villages of 500-1000 square foot houses and give them to those who can't afford a housing?
Old_Answer: Better idea. Why don’t we just build housing until it becomes cheap enough that anyone above the poverty line can afford? That means no matter how much you make housing will be cheaper. It’s a win win all around if your goal is to give everyone an affordable place to live. Giving stuff away for free simply creates different winners and losers. Sure it’s great for the person lucky enough to get one, but what about the guy who makes $1 too much. Maybe he makes rent every month, but just barely. Any type of accident or set back is going to devastate him though. He will now have the goal to make slightly less to qualify and those who did qualify certainly are going to want to stay under that limit. Government should come in and build shared infrastructure that’s open to everyone. Building private homes simply distorts a market that would naturally balance itself. This is not a hard problem, we simply need to build housing until it becomes affordable for anyone working the most menial of jobs full time. Doing anything else is stupid prior to fixing that issue.

Even if land is available, zoning laws and regulations often complicate the process, as many municipalities have strict guidelines about what can be built and where. Additionally, while the idea of small, affordable homes sounds appealing, the reality is that creating a sustainable community requires more than just housing; it necessitates infrastructure, access to services, and a supportive environment. These villages would need to include schools, healthcare, and transportation options, which can be costly and logistically challenging to implement. Furthermore, there’s the question of funding. While government grants and non-profit organizations could help, the scale of investment required to build and maintain these communities is substantial. There’s also the social aspect to consider; integrating these villages into existing communities can lead to resistance from current residents who may fear changes to their neighborhoods. Lastly, the long-term success of such initiatives depends on ongoing support and resources for residents, which can be difficult to sustain. In essence, while the vision of park-like villages is appealing, the complexities of land use, funding, community integration, and ongoing support create a daunting barrier to making this idea a reality.

Question: Why does the technology industry receive a disproportionate amount of flack about diversity when other occupations, such as recruitment consultant and warehouse operative, are reportedly more inhospitable to women?
Old_Answer: Why do people focus so much time on acts of terrorism when many more people die in automobile accidents? Why is Beyonce's pregnancy national news when having a child is commonplace? Whether you call it infamy or celebrity, the tech titans have a vaunted place in society. Everyone knows Google and Uber by name. They know what they do and interact with thier products on a daily basis. What's more, the engineering jobs are highly skilled creative pursuits that require motivation, dedication, and responsibility to create a working product and solve unique problems. If your workers are not motivated at a warehouse job, you can just hire some more workers and brute force it. It's a problem, but a more controllable one. If your software engineers make a bad product, it will be seen by customers and have a negative impact on more then just a few worker’s productivity. Culture is very important at tech companies where building a slightly better product can mean whether you survive or not. The perceived value of an engineer also comes from the success of the projects they work on and the visibility of them within the company. Performance is subjective and multiplied by the presence of the deliverables. You can't simply measure performance based on the the number of things you ship or the number of people who get hired from your recruitment activities. As an engineer, if you get put on a project that has a low potential upside, your career will see it's potential drop. Working on a tool to help a handful of administrative employees do thier job just doesn't have the reach of say working on search for Google. If you are made to feel uncomfortable on the project you are on, it may mean switching to a project with a less desirable career trajectory or even have to be down leveled. Switching divisions or jobs means not only a different evironment, but giving up a likely unique project that may hold outsized value to you. Diversity problems in tech companies have an exceptional effect on the company's bottom line, they have an exceptional effect on the employee’s career path, they have some exceptionally undiverse demographics, and the companies in question tend to be exceptionally famous. That doesnt mean diversity issues are unique to tech and if you are an individual experiencing them, it really doesn't matter which industry you are in to make it a problem. Tech is likely far from the most egregious industry. That being said, the tech industry does have a lot of reasons that make it a good place to evolve diversity in the workplace to the next level. Why not start a dialog there?
Answer_with_writing_sample: The technology industry often finds itself under a microscope regarding diversity, and while it may seem disproportionate compared to fields like recruitment consulting or warehouse operations, there are several reasons for this scrutiny. First, the tech sector is highly visible and influential, shaping the future of work and society at large. When tech giants like Google or Facebook are criticized for their lack of diversity, it resonates more broadly because these companies set trends and standards that ripple through other industries. Additionally, the tech industry has made bold claims about innovation and progress, which raises expectations around inclusivity. When these expectations aren’t met, the backlash is more pronounced. Moreover, the narrative surrounding tech is often one of meritocracy, where skills and talent should theoretically transcend gender and race. When this ideal fails to materialize, it highlights systemic issues that may not be as visible in other sectors. In contrast, industries like recruitment consulting or warehouse work may not have the same level of public discourse or expectation for diversity, leading to less scrutiny. Question: It's often said that if you raise corporate taxes, the business will leave for another state or country. What actually happens to the original state or nation's economy when this happens in the short and long-term?
Old_Answer: In the US the statutory corporate tax rate is relatively disconnected from the effective tax rate corporations pay. Significant changes to the corporate tax rate are almost always accompanied by equally significant changes to deductions and the closing of loopholes. Note both the sharp decline in the statutory rate in the mid 80s is accompanied not by a sharp decline in effective rates, but rather a substantial increase due to closed loopholes! The rest of the timeline is also very disconnected and illustrates that the statutory rate the government sets usually plays only a very tangential role in the effective taxes corporations pay. The health of the overall economy as well as how well corporations are able to restructure to take advantage of the tax code plays a much bigger role as well as the structure of the country’s tax code in question. That doesn’t mean that taxes don’t play a big role in shaping the economy, but the effects tend to be subtle and take decades to play out in ways that can only be completely understood in retrospect and are always way more complicated than as a direct result of a statutory rate change. Incentives and deliberately shaped loopholes tend to be a much bigger driver of where businesses move to. When it comes to taxes, the carrot tends to have way more of a shaping effect on the nation as a whole then the stick. The simple answer to your question as to what happens to the economy as the result of corporate taxes being raised in OECD countries is… nothing happens in the short term. Governments will go out of there way to make sure effective rate increases are minimized when the scrutiny is on after a statutory tax raise and any significant increases are phased in over long periods of time. In the long term, companies will adapt to the new tax code, sometimes in positive ways that match the intention of the behaviors the changes were trying to drive, sometimes in negative ways, the only thing that is clear is that the statutory increase that comes with major changes to the tax code is least predictive metric of the health of the future economy.
